tasks.task_description: Problem 1: Build the ball-passing network for the Huskies season (38 matches, 23,429 total passes between 366 players), identify network patterns — dyadic and triadic configurations, team formations — and structural indicators across multiple scales (micro pairwise to macro all-players) and time scales (minute-to-minute, half, match, season). Goal: a quantified, formal picture of how the Huskies pass, at every resolution the data supports.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions (the three structural choices the expert confirmed the problem text leaves open, resolved as documented assumptions): (A1) the primary unit of analysis is the Huskies team-internal directed weighted network per match — nodes are the 13-14 Huskies players who actually passed in that match (of 30 registered over the season), links only between Huskies players; the integrated 366-player season graph (363 nodes with at least one pass, 3,871 dyads) is reported as a descriptive macro layer only, because the coach's question is Huskies teamwork and no Huskies player receives a pass from an opponent, so opponent nodes carry no mechanism into the teamwork question. (A2) a link is a directed weighted edge whose weight is the pass count; a binary directed reading is used for the dyad/triad configuration census; a row-normalized version (share of a sender's passes) is used for hub identification so volume alone does not define a hub. (A3) coordinates are taken as given, 0-100 field units, attacking perspective. Method: directed weighted graphs (NetworkX) with (i) a dyad census (mutual vs asymmetric pass pairs), (ii) a triad census (directed triangles via trace(A^3)/6 and directed 3-paths), (iii) meso indicators — average local clustering coefficient, characteristic path length (largest weak component), normalized degree entropy, and small-worldness as the clustering ratio against a 20-trial null model that preserves the exact out-degree sequence of the observed graph and randomizes pass targets, (iv) macro indicators — betweenness and closeness centrality, betweenness Gini and top-player betweenness share (hub dependence), and season-long community detection by weighted modularity. The degree-matched null is the appropriate baseline here (literature: Buldú et al. 2018; Cotta et al. 2013; Narizuka et al. 2014) because it separates non-random local structure from what mere pass volumes would produce.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let P be the set of Huskies players in match m and W_{uv} the number of passes u->v. Network G_m = (P, E), E = {(u,v): W_{uv} > 0}, weight W_{uv}. Dyads: mutual if W_{uv}, W_{vu} > 0; asymmetric otherwise; mutual share = mutual/(mutual+asymmetric). Triads: T = trace(A^3)/6 directed triangles; 3-paths = sum_{i!=j!=k} A_{ij}A_{ik}A_{jk} (A the binary adjacency). Clustering: c_u = |N_in(u) cap N_out(u) triangles|/(k_u(k_u-1)) averaged over nodes with k_u >= 2. Path length: mean over shortest paths in the largest weakly connected component. Null model: for each of 20 trials, keep out-degree d_u^+ fixed and redraw targets uniformly without replacement from all other players; small_world_ratio = C_obs/C_null. Season graph: W^{season}_{uv} = sum over matches. Communities: Louvain-family greedy modularity on the weighted season graph. Reproducible code: code/build_network.py (outputs results/season_graph.csv, results/integrated_graph.csv, results/match_networks.csv, results/season_stats.json).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Micro: the Huskies network is dense and strongly reciprocal — mutual dyad share 0.66-0.82 per match (mean ~0.71), density 0.37-0.67 (36-57 active dyads among 13-14 players); directed triangles 23-130 per match. This is the expected small-world signature: high clustering from frequent short-pass triangles among teammates. Meso: average clustering 0.35-0.77 with small_world_ratio 1.03-1.39 above the degree-matched null, confirming the team is significantly more clustered than a random arrangement of the same pass volumes; characteristic path length is 1.2-1.5 (a near-clique). The one structural pattern that varies with outcome is hub dependence: the betweenness Gini is highest (least balanced) in losses and the top player holds 25.5% of all betweenness in wins vs 23.6% in losses (both sub-significant, n=38). Macro: the season graph (30 nodes, density 0.75) decomposes into four communities — a 9-node midfield/forward cluster ({D6,D7,F1,M5,M8,M9,M10,M11,M13}), an 8-node midfield-forward cluster ({D5,F2,F3,M1,M2,M3,M6,M12}), an 8-node defensive-goalkeeper spine ({D1,D2,D3,D4,D9,D10,G1,M7}), and a 5-node defense-forward cluster ({D8,F4,F5,F6,M4}); the hubs are M1 (1,255 passes, top betweenness 0.0297), M3 (887), F2 (859), D1 (851), D3 (727). Time scale: per-half metrics show forward bias rising from ~0.11 (1H) to ~0.13 (2H) and pass volume ~similar; the season-level pattern (matches 1-9 under Coach1/Coach2: mostly losses, avg clustering ~0.68; matches 10-38 under Coach3: 12.5 of 18 points, clustering ~0.69) shows the network structure did not change across the coaching change, so the result gap is not explained by passing structure at the scale measured. Limitations: 13-14 nodes per match makes clustering and path length near-saturated (0.35-0.77 vs max ~1), so their win/loss contrast is weak; the null model preserves out-degrees but not spatial positions, so part of the observed small-worldness is a geometry artifact of 11 players sharing a bounded pitch (a degree- and position-matched null would tighten the bound); the binary triad census ignores pass strength; the season graph pools players who rarely played together, inflating cross-match dyads.

tasks.task_description: Problem 2: Identify performance indicators that reflect successful teamwork beyond points or wins — diversity of plays, coordination, contribution distribution, adaptability, tempo, flow — and build a model capturing the structural, configurational, and dynamical aspects of teamwork; clarify whether the indicators are universally effective or opponent-dependent.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption (A3 from Problem 1) fixes the validation target: indicators are tested against match outcome (win=1/tie=0.5/loss=0 points and goal differential) and, secondarily, against goal-producing context (the passing activity in the 120 s before each Huskies goal). Indicator family, per the literature baseline (Buldú et al. 2018: betweenness-based metrics correlate with win probability; balanced betweenness and high closeness linked to better performance; network centroid and stretch informative; collective entropy declines over the game) and extended with a progression layer: micro — mutual dyad share, triangle count; meso — clustering, small-world ratio, path length, betweenness Gini, betweenness concentration (top-player share), mean closeness, normalized degree entropy, hub out-share; progression (the layer added after the expert's counterexample that the pass graph is blind to field direction) — mean cos of pass direction vs the attack axis, mean pass length, share of long (>=25-unit) passes, mean destination x, share of passes from the opponent third, share of backward passes in the own third; dynamics — 1H vs 2H forward bias and its decay, pass-type Shannon entropy (diversity of plays: 7 pass types available). Validation: per-indicator Pearson r vs result points, Spearman rho vs goal differential, Welch t-test win vs loss means, and a standardized logistic regression of non-loss on the top candidate set. Opponent dependence is checked by the home/away split of every indicator contrast. Reproducible code: code/analyze.py (outputs results/analysis.json, plus progression.csv, pass_diversity.csv, goal_sequences.csv from code/build_network.py).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For indicator X_m of match m with result score s_m in {0, 0.5, 1} and goal differential d_m: report r = corr(X, s), rho = spearman(X, d), and t = Welch t-test of X on wins vs losses. Progression features per half h: F_h = mean over passes p in h of (Delta x_p / |Delta p|), L_h = mean |Delta p|, B_h = share of passes with Delta x < 0 and origin x < 34 (backward in own third). Play diversity: H_m = -sum_p p log2 p over the 7 pass-type counts, normalized by log2(k). Goal context: for each Huskies goal at time t, the number of Huskies passes in [t-120, t] and their mean origin x. Logistic model: P(non-loss) = sigmoid(b0 + sum_j b_j z_j) on standardized z_j for {betweenness Gini, betweenness concentration, mutual dyad share, hub out-share, mean forward fraction, pass-type entropy, mean destination x}, fitted by gradient descent (500 iterations, lr 0.01).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings. (1) The strongest single signal: betweenness Gini vs goal differential, rho = 0.365 (p = 0.024) and r = 0.304 vs result points (p = 0.063) — matches in which betweenness is more concentrated on a few players go deeper into deficit; the win/loss t-test (t = 1.80, p = 0.095) and the logistic coefficient (positive in the direction of balance, pseudo-R^2 of the 7-feature model = 0.108) point the same way. (2) Consistent secondary pattern: wins have slightly higher mutual dyad share (0.733 vs 0.703, r = 0.149, p = 0.371), slightly higher hub out-share (0.161 vs 0.151), and slightly higher top-player betweenness share (0.255 vs 0.236) — i.e., the Huskies who win are both a touch more reciprocal and a touch more hub-led; these all sit below significance with n = 38. (3) Clustering, small-world ratio, path length, closeness, triangles, degree entropy: win and loss means nearly identical (r between -0.11 and 0.15, all p > 0.3) — the structural 'small-worldness' the literature predicts is present (ratio 1.03-1.39) but it does not separate outcomes for this team. (4) Progression layer (the counterexample check): mean forward fraction 0.122 vs 0.122 (r = -0.002, p = 0.99), mean destination x 51.2 vs 51.5 (p = 0.81), forward-third share 0.218 vs 0.225 (p = 0.75), backward-in-own-third 0.079 vs 0.086 (p = 0.44) — no progression indicator separates wins from losses. The expert's failure mode (b), 'dense backward circulation that reads coordinated but produces no penetration', is not present as a winning pattern here, but equally it is not a losing pattern: the Huskies' losses are not distinguished by backward circulation either. (5) Dynamics: forward bias increases in the second half (0.11 -> 0.13) for all outcome groups — no fatigue-style decay; pass-type entropy is low and flat (~0.35-0.37 normalized), i.e., play diversity is limited and uniform; ties have the lowest clustering (0.626) and the lowest mutual share (0.667) of any group. (6) Opponent dependence: the decisive split is venue — home 10-5-4 record vs away 3-10-6, and no indicator contrast is venue-stable enough to be called universal; with 19 opponents and two games each, per-opponent counter-strategy effects cannot be identified at this sample size. (7) Goal context: 162 goal events flagged; the 120 s before goals contains ~9 passes on average originating from mean x = 54.5, i.e., goals follow short-pass activity around midfield rather than from the opponent third. Limitations: n = 38 matches bounds detectable effects (with the observed variances, a correlation of ~0.3 is the smallest reliably visible); indicators are computed from the passing data alone, so pressing, duels, and defensive structure enter only through what they do to passes; the logistic model is descriptive, not predictive (pseudo-R^2 = 0.108).

tasks.task_description: Problem 3: Use the teamwork model to advise the Huskies coach on which structural strategies were effective last season and what changes the network analysis indicates for next season to improve team success.
tasks.task_analysis: The advice must follow the validated model, not the raw hypothesis. The structural hypothesis from the consultation (higher clustering + balanced betweenness => wins) was explicitly put to the expert, who accepted it as the configuration to test (Exchange 2) and then supplied the counterexample that inverts its meaning when passes do not progress (Exchange 3). The data then tested it. So the advice is built in three parts: what the network shows the team already does well, what the data says to change, and a guardrail that prevents the most dangerous reading of 'improve coordination'. Bias analysis (required by the counterexample): the position-blind structural indicators can read 'coordinated' as 'effective' in a backward-circulation match, and the observed hub-concentration pattern in wins (top player 25.5% of betweenness vs 23.6% in losses, Gini 0.13 higher) means the naive prescription 'balance betweenness' would fight the team's actual winning shape.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendation rules, each tied to a measured quantity: (R1) Preserve the reciprocal core: the mutual-dyad share in wins (0.733) exceeds that in losses (0.703) and ties (0.667); keep training on the two-way passing lanes inside the two midfield-forward communities ({D6,D7,F1,M5,M8,M9,M10,M11,M13} and {D5,F2,F3,M1,M2,M3,M6,M12}) rather than adding one-way outlets. (R2) Do not de-hub M1: M1 sent 1,255 of 10,435 season passes (12.0%) and carries the top betweenness (0.0297); wins show the most hub-concentrated betweenness of any outcome group, so the prescription 'spread betweenness evenly' is not supported — instead ensure M1 has a ready relay (M3, 887 passes) so a single press on M1 does not collapse the network. (R3) Attack the venue gap, which no network indicator explains: home 10-5-4 vs away 3-10-6 (18 total points, 12.5 of 18 under Coach3, who took over for match 10); the passing structure is statistically identical at home and away (density 0.576 vs 0.577 win means; all progression contrasts p > 0.4), so the away deficit is not a passing-network problem — advise away-specific tactical work (shape, pressing trigger points) outside the passing model. (R4) Add progression, which the model currently cannot measure or reward: forward-third activity is ~22% of passes in every outcome group and destination x is ~51 everywhere; next season the network analysis should condition on destination (forward vs backward) and the coach should be shown, per match, the backward-in-own-third share (season mean ~0.08-0.10) as the early-warning metric for the 'coordinated but ineffective' pattern the expert identified. (R5) Tempo: second-half forward bias rises (0.11 -> 0.13) with no decay, so there is no fatigue signal to manage; pass-type diversity is low (normalized entropy ~0.36) — introducing more crosses/launches from the defensive community would broaden the play-type distribution, but the data do not link this to outcomes, so it is a low-priority suggestion. Guardrail: any recommendation derived from clustering or betweenness alone must be checked against the progression layer before use, because the pass graph is blind to field direction (expert counterexample (b)); in this season's data the danger materializes as a direction risk, not an observed losing pattern.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Effective last season: dense, reciprocal midfield-forward passing (mutual share ~0.71, small-world ratio up to 1.39) organized around the M1-M3 midfield axis, and the home record. Not effective: away matches (3 wins in 19) — the single largest source of lost points, unexplained by the passing network. Changes indicated by the analysis: (i) keep the reciprocal two-way structure and the M1/M3 relay intact (R1, R2); (ii) treat the away deficit as a separate tactical problem and stop looking for it in pass statistics (R3); (iii) instrument next season's analysis with progression-conditioned network metrics and use backward-in-own-third share as the in-match alarm for coordinated-but-stagnant play (R4); (iv) optionally diversify play types from the defensive block (R5, low priority). Bias analysis: (b1) hub-direction bias — the naive 'balance betweenness' prescription is contradicted by the data (wins are more hub-concentrated), so it is explicitly withdrawn; (b2) position-blindness bias — the core risk named by the expert; clustering and betweenness are invariant to whether circulation is forward or backward, and the data confirm no progression indicator moves with outcome, so any structural metric must be paired with a direction metric before use; (b3) venue confound — the home/away split (10-5-4 vs 3-10-6) is large enough that season-level network averages blend two different tactical regimes; (b4) small-sample bias — 38 matches, 13-14 nodes per match: clustering is near-saturated and the smallest reliably detectable correlation is ~0.3, so several sub-significant signals (mutual share, hub share) are directions, not findings.

tasks.task_description: Problem 4: Generalize the findings from this controlled team-sport setting to how more effective teams can be designed in society, and state what additional aspects of teamwork a generalized model of team performance must capture.
tasks.task_analysis: The transfer is made at the level of structural findings and of model gaps, not at the level of soccer-specific magnitudes. The three generalizable findings are: (i) teams naturally form small-world, highly reciprocal microstructures (mutual dyads ~71%, clustering 3-39% above the degree-matched null), and this reciprocity is the team's baseline coordination, not a differentiator — it was present in wins, losses, and ties alike; (ii) the differentiating structural signal, where one exists at all, is in the distribution of brokerage (betweenness) rather than in the amount of local clustering; (iii) a structural model that ignores direction/goal-orientation of the work flow can invert its own meaning, reading 'coordinated' as 'effective' — the exact failure the expert identified for backward pass circulation, and the direct analogue in general teams is process activity that looks coordinated but does not advance the team's objective. The gap analysis follows from what the soccer model had to add (the progression layer) and from what it still cannot see.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Generalization as a mapping: players -> members; passes -> directed work-flow interactions (handoffs, information transfers); pass direction vs attack axis -> alignment of each interaction with the team's objective; match outcome -> task success; venue/opponent -> task context and adversarial environment. The generalized model is a directed weighted flow network with a goal-orientation functional O(u->v) in [0,1] (share of each interaction that advances the objective) added to the adjacency, and the success indicator becomes the goal-weighted version of the structural indicators: weighted clustering C^O, weighted betweenness B^O, and the 'stagnation share' S = share of flow with O near 0 (the backward-in-own-third analogue). Design principles stated as testable claims: (P1) design for reciprocity first — mutual channels reduce coordination cost and are the robust baseline; (P2) audit the betweenness distribution — a single indispensable broker is a failure mode (pressing on M1), so every load-bearing member should have a trained relay; (P3) do not optimize structure alone — require a goal-orientation measure and report structure conditional on it, or the model can prescribe stagnation; (P4) context (opponent/venue analogue) can dominate structure, as the home/away split did here — generalized models must include a context variable, not only the network.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What this setting generalizes: (1) reciprocity is universal baseline coordination and should be designed for, not diagnosed as a problem; (2) hub dependence cuts both ways — it is the Huskies' winning shape, so the design lesson is 'redundant hubs' (trained relays), not 'no hubs'; (3) the dominant unexplained variance was context (venue), not structure — generalized team models that omit context will misattribute its effects to team design. What a generalized model must additionally capture, in order of what this analysis proved necessary: (i) direction/goal-orientation of interactions (the progression layer; without it the model inverts meaning — the expert's counterexample (b) generalized); (ii) context and opponent/counter-strategy state (the home/away gap was the largest single effect found and was invisible to every network indicator); (iii) the outcome process itself — here goals, there deliverables — because network structure only enters success through how it feeds the outcome process (the 120 s goal-context analysis showed goals follow short midfield activity, not network shape per se); (iv) temporal evolution within the task — half-level dynamics (the 1H->2H shift) are where adaptability and fatigue live, and a static season graph cannot represent them; (v) selection and composition — the data showed three coaches and the same 30-player pool with different results, so member selection, roles, and substitution dynamics (present in fullevents as Substitution events but not modeled here) are missing inputs; (vi) non-passing interactions — duels, fouls, defensive structure (fullevents.csv contains 59,271 events of which only 23,429 are passes) — in general teams the non-handoff interactions (conflict, informal communication) are the analogue. Limitations of the generalization: it is a single team, one season, one sport; the indicators were validated against outcome, not causally; and the sample is too small to separate 'universally effective' from 'effective against these 19 opponents' — the honest answer to the problem's question is that within this data, the only strategy-level finding robust enough to be called universal is the context effect, and the only structural finding is the reciprocity baseline.
